early-newborn-conversation.title: Begin with your voice
early-newborn-conversation.invitation: Say a few words, then wait for a sound or gesture.
early-newborn-conversation.summary: Use your baby’s name and tell them what is happening. Pause so a sound or gesture can become part of the conversation.
early-newborn-conversation.cue: You are holding or caring for your baby, with a moment to talk and listen.
detail: A bath about to begin, the part of the body being washed, or the room you are entering can give you something to talk about. Use the words you know and speak gently.

Let your baby see your face. After saying something, wait and notice their response. You might echo a sound or answer a gesture, then leave another pause. The book treats these early exchanges as conversation.
If your baby has an older sibling, another conversation can begin while that child plays: with the baby awake, talk about what their sibling is doing.

early-read-aloud.title: Read a little of your book aloud
early-read-aloud.invitation: Read a little aloud from something you enjoy.
early-read-aloud.summary: In the first few months, a book you want to read can become something to share: read it aloud with your baby nearby.
early-read-aloud.cue: You have something you would enjoy reading and your baby is awake and comfortable.
detail: Davies and Uzodike describe early reading as a chance to hear the sounds and rhythm of language. The book does not have to be a baby book; you can read from one that interests you.
Simple picture books are another option. If a picture catches your baby’s attention, you can describe it or stay with that page.

baby-movement.title: Room for their own movement
baby-movement.invitation: The authors make room for the baby’s own awake movement, with comfort and help close by.
baby-movement.summary: The authors favor awake movement that the baby initiates, with room to explore, help when needed, and no propping into sitting or standing before they can get there themselves.
baby-movement.cue: Notice how your baby moves now, what catches their attention, and when effort becomes frustration.
detail: Davies and Uzodike describe a prepared space where a baby can explore their own movements. A nearby object may invite a reach or a change of direction; the point is to follow the baby’s present interest and pace.

Their caution is about propping a baby into sitting or standing. They separately describe awake time on both the back and tummy, while noticing discomfort and changing things or picking the baby up when needed.

When effort turns to frustration, they describe coming closer and offering enough help for the baby to continue. Their activity ages are guides, and they explicitly welcome seeking support for developmental concerns.
